content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In popular Christian teaching, lamp oil is most commonly taken as a symbol of the Holy Spirit (and, closely related, the inner spiritual life or grace supplied by the Spirit that keeps one's 'light' burning). This reading is driven above all by the Parable of the Ten Virgins, where possessing oil marks readiness for the Bridegroom's coming, and it is reinforced by the broader biblical association of anointing oil with the Spirit's presence and empowerment.", "primary_basis": ["Matthew 25:1-13 (Parable of the Ten Virgins: wise virgins have oil, foolish do not)", "Exodus 27:20-21 and Leviticus 24:1-4 (pure olive oil for the perpetually burning tabernacle lamp)", "Zechariah 4:1-6, 11-14 (golden lampstand fed by olive trees: 'not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit')", "1 Samuel 16:13 (Samuel anoints David with oil and the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him mightily)", "Acts 10:38 (God 'anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power')", "1 John 2:20, 27 (the 'anointing' from the Holy One that abides in believers)", "Psalm 45:7 / Hebrews 1:9 ('anointed with the oil of gladness')", "Isaiah 61:1 / Luke 4:18 ('the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me')"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Personal faith, genuine saving grace, or a real (versus merely professed) relationship with Christ — the oil distinguishes true disciples from nominal ones; common in Reformed and evangelical exegesis of Matthew 25, sometimes deliberately avoiding a one-to-one allegorical identification.", "basis": ["Matthew 25:1-13", "Matthew 7:21-23 (profession without reality)", "2 Timothy 3:5 (form of godliness denying its power)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Good works, love/charity, or deeds of righteousness that accompany true faith; found in patristic writers (e.g., Augustine, Chrysostom on the Ten Virgins) and in some later homiletic traditions.", "basis": ["Matthew 25:1-13 read alongside Matthew 5:16 ('let your light shine before others, that they may see your good works')", "James 2:14-26 (faith without works)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Spiritual preparedness or watchfulness itself — oil as a narrative device signifying readiness for Christ's return rather than a coded symbol for any single referent; many modern critical commentators warn against allegorizing the detail at all.", "basis": ["Matthew 25:13 ('watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour')", "Matthew 24:42-44"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "The Word of God / divine truth that fuels the believer's light.", "basis": ["Psalm 119:105 ('your word is a lamp to my feet')", "Proverbs 6:23"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Individually acquired spiritual experience, obedience, and testimony that cannot be borrowed or transferred (a reading emphasized in Latter-day Saint teaching, e.g., Spencer W. Kimball's exposition of the Ten Virgins).", "basis": ["Matthew 25:8-9 (the oil cannot be shared)", "Doctrine and Covenants 45:56-57 (LDS scripture explicitly linking oil to receiving the truth and taking the Holy Spirit as guide)"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": false, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is a strong, widely recognizable popular association of lamp oil with the Holy Spirit, grounded in the Bible's pervasive anointing imagery, and this is arguably the default meaning in devotional, Pentecostal/charismatic, and much evangelical teaching. However, academic and confessional commentary on Matthew 25 is genuinely divided: many scholars (e.g., in the tradition of Jülicher and most modern critical commentators) resist assigning the oil any specific symbolic referent, treating it as a plot detail signifying preparedness, while patristic and Reformation-era interpreters variously identified it with charity, good works, faith, or grace. So the Holy Spirit reading is dominant at the popular level but not a settled scholarly consensus; the safest characterization is 'dominant in popular usage, contested in exegesis.' Related but distinct oil symbolism (healing, consecration, gladness, kingship) exists for anointing oil generally and should not be conflated with lamp-oil symbolism specifically."}
